d.g: To walk around something in a circle, especially for a ritual purpose.
d.x: Circumambulate the city of a dreamy Sabbath afternoon.

circumambulate.e: Latin circumambulatus, past participle of circumambulare (“to walk around”). Equivalent to circum- + ambulate.

d.g: To surgically remove the foreskin (prepuce) from the penis of.
To surgically remove the clitoris (clitoridectomy), clitoral hood, or labia.
To trim off the portion of the barrel liner of a large-caliber naval gun that protrudes from the end of the barrel as a result of the liner slowly stretching from prolonged fire.

circumcise.e: From Middle English circumcisen, from Old French circumciser (modern French circoncire) and its etymon Latin circumcīsus, the past participle of circumcīdō (“cut around”), from circum (“about, around; through”) + caedō (“cut, hew”).

d.g: To pour round; to spread round, as a fluid.
To spread round; to surround.

circumfuse.e: Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker-der. Ancient Greek κίρκος (kírkos)bor. Latin circus Latin circum Latin circum-bor. English circum- English fuse English circumfuse From circum- + fuse.

d.g: To travel completely around somewhere or something, especially by sail.
d.x: We circumnavigated the Mediterranean.

d.g: To circumvent or bypass.
d.x: Rebel of the tournament: Saudi Arabia’s Malek Al Hawsawi, who circumnavigated Fifa’s ban on jewellery by keeping his ring in his mouth.

d.g: To sail around the world.
d.x: Jack and Lura Francis, both fairly tall, circumnavigated on a Westsail 32.

circumnavigate.e: Borrowed from Latin circumnāvigātus, perfect passive participle of circumnāvigō (“sail round something, circumnavigate”), from circum (“about, around”) + nāvigō (“sail, navigate”), from nāvis (“ship”) + agō (“do”). By surface analysis, circum- + navigate.

d.g: To draw a line around; to encircle.
To limit narrowly; to restrict.
To draw the smallest circle or higher-dimensional sphere that has (a polyhedron, polygon, etc.) in its interior.

circumscribe.e: From Latin circumscrībō, from circum (“around”) + scrībō (“write”). By surface analysis, circum- + scribe.

d.g: To describe, verify or prove by setting out circumstantial evidence
d.x: Neither will time permit to circumstantiate these particulars, which I have only touched in the general.

d.g: To place in particular circumstances; to invest with particular accidents or adjuncts.
d.x: If the act were otherwise circumstantiated, it might will that freely which now it wills reluctantly.

d.g: To surround with, or as if with, a rampart.
d.x: The settlement is circumvallated by a stake-fence, so decayed that one may gain ingress at a dozen places.

d.g: Surrounded with a wall; enclosed with a rampart.
Surrounded by a ridge or elevation.

circumvallate.e: From Latin circumvallare, from circum- + vallum (“rampart”).

d.g: to avoid or get around something; to bypass
to surround or besiege
to outwit or outsmart

To move or revolve around something.
